While the exit_on_error=False parameter was introduced to allow users to catch parsing errors instead of having the program terminate, its implementation has historically been inconsistent [1][2][3]. In many cases, ArgumentParser still calls the internal error method, which by default invokes sys.exit with a status code of 2 [4][5]. For a significant period following the introduction of exit_on_error in Python 3.9, the setting only affected specific types of validation errors (such as type or choice mismatches), while other errors—such as unrecognized arguments or missing required arguments—continued to trigger the default error behavior that exits the program [1][2][3]. To ensure robust error handling, developers have often needed to subclass ArgumentParser and override the error method to raise a custom exception instead of relying solely on the exit_on_error parameter [5][6]. def inspect_header(path: Path, definition: DatasetDefinition) -> tuple[str, ...]:
    try:
        with gzip.open(path, mode="rt", encoding="utf-8-sig", newline="") as handle:
            reader = csv.reader(handle)
            header = next(reader)
    except (OSError, EOFError, UnicodeError, csv.Error, StopIteration) as exc:
        raise DatasetSchemaError(
            f"unable to read {definition.filename}: {exc}"
        ) from exc
    duplicates = sorted({name for name in header if header.count(name) > 1})
    if duplicates:
        raise DatasetSchemaError(
            f"{definition.filename} has duplicate columns: {', '.join(duplicates)}",
        )
    missing = set(definition.required) - set(header)
    if missing:
        raise DatasetSchemaError(
            f"{definition.filename} missing required columns: {', '.join(sorted(missing))}",
        )
    return tuple(column for column in header if column not in definition.required)
```

💡 Result:

No, the ArgumentParser.error method does not always raise SystemExit when exit_on_error is set to False, but in many versions of Python, it may still trigger an exit depending on the specific type of error encountered [1][2][3]. While the exit_on_error=False parameter was introduced to allow users to catch parsing errors instead of having the program terminate, its implementation has historically been inconsistent [1][2][3]. In many cases, ArgumentParser still calls the internal error method, which by default invokes sys.exit with a status code of 2 [4][5]. For a significant period following the introduction of exit_on_error in Python 3.9, the setting only affected specific types of validation errors (such as type or choice mismatches), while other errors—such as unrecognized arguments or missing required arguments—continued to trigger the default error behavior that exits the program [1][2][3]. To ensure robust error handling, developers have often needed to subclass ArgumentParser and override the error method to raise a custom exception instead of relying solely on the exit_on_error parameter [5][6]. If you require non-exiting behavior for all possible errors, overriding the error method remains the most reliable approach [5][6].

    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
